newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO ministers weigh up ties with Russia.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers weigh up ties with Russia.

text.p: NATO defence ministers were set on Thursday to tell Russia's Igor Rodionov that the alliance would press ahead with enlargement, against Moscow's wishes, to take in its former communist allies in Europe.
But the ministers were also to tell the Russian defence minister that NATO wanted enlargement to move in parallel with building a new relationship with Moscow.
The NATO ministers were meeting informally in this Norwegian port city to evaluate relations with the former Cold War adversary and former Soviet satellites in eastern and central Europe.
Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and perhaps Slovenia, are likely to become the alliance's first new members since Spain and Portugal joined in the late 1970s.
The issue has infuriated Moscow and left the allies pondering what they tell those now-independent former Soviet satellites which have not measured up to early NATO membership.
The ministers on Thursday reviewed ways of reinforcing their Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme designed to fill a security vacuum in Europe after the collapse of communism.
NATO officials say the allies want to upgrade PFP to help smooth the ruffled feathers of countries which fail to gain membership of the Atlantic Alliance next year.
At the very least, countries like the Baltic states want a promise that they can have membership at a later date.

The NATO defence chiefs also discussed reforms to the alliance's command structures which would allow Moscow to position liaison officers at various levels, building on the current cooperation in the alliance's peace mission in Bosnia.
On Wednesday, NATO decided to start planning for a possible follow-on force when the mandate of the 52,000-strong peace Implementation Force (IFOR) expires this December.
All NATO capitals want Russia to participate in the new force.
"The dialogue between NATO and Russia will be very intense. We will have an open dialogue, a frank dialogue," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said.

A senior U.S. defence official earlier this week said Defence Secretary William Perry looked forward to private talks with Rodionov on continued cooperation -- following on from the close ties he developed with former Russian Defence Minister Pavel Grachev who was sacked in a government shakeup in July.
Perry has said he understands Russia's concerns about NATO expansion and that he strongly supports proposals for a new NATO charter giving Moscow a non-voting voice in alliance affairs.
